title: Research
text: Though social behavior and immune function have historically been studied separately, there is increasing evidence to demonstrate how inextricably linked these two systems are. My research has focused on the bidirectional relationship between social behavior and the immune system, and the mechanistic link between the two.

title: Research
section: How does the social environment shape responses to immune challenges?
text:
How does the social environment shape responses to immune challenges?
Social environments can both protect individuals from immune challenges and create unique risks. For animals living in social groups, relationships with conspecifics can provide access to resources, protection from predators, and social support. At the same time, increased social contact can increase exposure to pathogens. How, then, does the immune system adapt to different social environments?
I have explored this question by examining wound healing in California mice living in social versus isolated conditions and investigating whether oxytocin—a hormone closely associated with social relationships—contributes to this response. I found that oxytocin impaired wound healing in socially isolated individuals, but not in socially housed individuals. These findings suggest that the physiological effects of oxytocin depend on an individual’s social environment and highlight one mechanism through which social context may shape immune function.

title: Research
section: How does the immune system shape social behavior?
text:
How does the immune system shape social behavior?
Immune activation can alter social behavior in diverse and context-dependent ways. Although sickness has traditionally been associated with social withdrawal, animals do not always respond to an immune challenge by avoiding others. In social species, immune activation can instead increase affiliation, depending on factors such as the relationship between individuals, social status, and the nature of the immune challenge. What determines whether an animal withdraws from others or seeks social contact when its immune system is activated?
I addressed this question by examining how California mice alter their social decisions following an inflammatory challenge with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Rather than producing a uniform decrease in social behavior, the response depended on the animals’ existing social phenotype. In males, individuals that were less affiliative prior to immune challenge showed the greatest subsequent increase in affiliation. These findings suggest that sickness behavior is not a fixed behavioral program, but instead depends on an individual’s social history and current social context.

title: Research
section: What biological mechanisms link the social and immune systems?
text:
What biological mechanisms link the social and immune systems?
The reciprocal relationship between social behavior and immune function raises a fundamental mechanistic question: how does information about the social environment reach the immune system, and how does immune activity ultimately influence the neural circuits that regulate social behavior?
My research investigates this interface through two candidate mechanisms: oxytocin signaling and microglia. Although oxytocin is best known for its role in social behavior, it also interacts extensively with the immune system and is released during inflammatory challenges. My work demonstrates that its effects on immune function depend on social context: during social isolation, oxytocin can impair wound healing rather than promote recovery.
I also investigate microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, as a potential pathway through which peripheral immune activity can influence social behavior. I found that greater microglial activation in the medial prefrontal cortex was associated with reduced social proximity following an inflammatory challenge. My current work moves from correlation toward causation by experimentally manipulating microglia both broadly and within the prefrontal cortex. By determining whether altering microglial function changes social responses to immune challenge, I aim to identify a mechanistic bridge between immune state, neural function, and social behavior.

title: Antiracism Learning and Action in Neuroscience
text:
For four years, I was the chair of Antiracism Learning and Action in Neuroscience (ALAN), a graduate student group focused on translating conversations about equity in science into concrete action. Through ALAN, I have developed and supported initiatives aimed at reducing barriers to scientific training, building connections between scientists and the broader community, and creating more inclusive academic environments.
After graduate school, I plan to continue working on antiracist and equity-focused initiatives, and I am always interested in collaboration. Please do not hesitate to reach out about working together!

title: Antiracism Learning and Action in Neuroscience
text:
Science Expo
The ALAN Science Expo is an annual outreach program developed in collaboration with Madison East High School. The event brings high school students together with researchers from across STEM for hands-on experiments, conversations about scientific careers, and opportunities to interact with scientists from
The goal of the Expo is to show a diverse group of students that scientists can share their identities and experiences—whether related to race, disability, gender, sexual orientation, or other aspects of identity—and to help students envision themselves as scientists even if they do not fit stereotypical ideas of what a “scientist” looks like.
Learn more about the Science Expo →

title: Antiracism Learning and Action in Neuroscience
text:
Expanding Access to Research
ALAN developed a Research and Job Opportunity Catalog for Underrepresented Undergraduates to make pathways into scientific research more transparent. This resource compiles laboratories recruiting undergraduate researchers, application guidance, post-baccalaureate opportunities, and other information that can otherwise be difficult to find without prior knowledge of academic systems.
The catalog also provides guidance on evaluating whether a lab is a safe and supportive environment, what to do when it is not, and highlights laboratories that have demonstrated a commitment to creating inclusive research environments.
Explore ALAN’s Research & Job Opportunity Catalog →

title: Antiracism Learning and Action in Neuroscience
section: Making the Hidden Curriculum More Visible
text:
Making the Hidden Curriculum More Visible
ALAN’s Grad Guide was developed to help incoming graduate students navigate aspects of graduate school that are often learned informally, including funding, teaching, mentor–mentee relationships, conflict, and the hidden curriculum. It also directs students toward resources for mental health, disability accommodations, reporting bias, and other forms of support.
Explore the Grad Guide →

title: Antiracism Learning and Action in Neuroscience
text:
Disability in STEM Symposium
With financial support from the HHMI Gilliam fellowship and from ALAN, I hosted a day-long free conference in 2025 including talks, workshops, and discussions focused on the experience of being disabled in STEM, how disability is commonly talked (or not talked) about in STEM communities, and the work people are doing to ensure that disabled voices are heard and how to make STEM more accessible. We had over 100 attendees, and the positive feedback we received demonstrated an interest and a need for more disability-centered conversations in STEM.

title: About
text:
I am a PhD candidate and HHMI Gilliam Fellow in the Marler Lab at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. I study how internal physiological states shape social decision-making. Using approaches from behavioral neuroscience and neuroimmunology in monogamous California mice, my research explores how immune signaling, social environments, and functional neuroplasticity interact to shape behavior. Ultimately, I aim to understand how the immune system acts not simply in response to disease, but as an active regulator of social behavior.
I received my B.S. from the University of Wisconsin–Madison. As an undergraduate in Dr. David Abbott’s lab, I studied how the menstrual cycle influences prosocial decision-making in rhesus macaques. This work sparked my interest in how peripheral physiological systems contribute to complex social behavior and ultimately led me to investigate interactions between the immune system, brain, and social environment.
As I move into the next stage of my research, I am interested in extending my work on the bidirectional relationship between immune function and social behavior to broader, ecologically relevant contexts. I want to understand how animals adapt their behavior to the diverse immune and environmental challenges they encounter in natural environments. At the cellular level, I am interested in how microglia interact with neural circuits to adaptively modify behavior in response to these challenges. At the social level, I want to explore how environmental and immune challenges experienced by individuals can propagate through social groups and reshape social networks. By connecting processes across these scales, I hope to understand how neuroimmune mechanisms contribute to adaptive behavior in complex social and ecological environments.
